questions.q: What does retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) add to a language model?
questions.why: RAG looks up your own documents for each question and gives them to the model, so answers rest on current, real sources.

questions.q: A RAG assistant confidently cites a policy that doesn't exist. What is this called?
questions.why: The model produced something plausible but false. Grounding checks and citations are how you catch it.

questions.q: Users say the assistant's answers are out of date. What do you check first?
options: Whether the document index is fresh
questions.why: In RAG, stale answers usually mean stale documents. Re-indexing is cheap; retraining is not.

questions.q: In RAG, 'chunking' means:
questions.why: Documents are cut into small passages so the right piece can be found and passed to the model.

questions.q: Which measure best shows that RAG answers are grounded?
options: Share of claims backed by sources
questions.why: Grounding is about whether each claim traces to a retrieved source, not speed or volume.

questions.q: End of PI Planning day 1: Team A's draft plan needs 140% of its capacity. What should the RTE do first?
options: Ask the team to plan overtime
Take it to the management review so scope or priorities change
Cut the team's lowest-value features yourself
Accept it and watch the system demos
questions.why: Day-1 management review exists for exactly this trade-off. The RTE surfaces it; Business Owners and Product Management decide what moves.

questions.q: The confidence vote ends with an average of 2 out of 5. What happens next?
options: Address the concerns and replan until confidence is acceptable
questions.why: Low confidence means the plan isn't believable. Hear the concerns, adjust, and vote again before committing.

questions.q: On the ART planning board, Team X's feature depends on Team Y, but Team Y has nothing planned for it. Best move?
options: Leave it, the teams will sort it out
Get both teams together now to agree a date or log it as a risk
Drop the feature from the PI
questions.why: An unplanned dependency is a hidden risk. Resolve it face to face during planning, when it's cheapest to fix.

questions.q: In ROAM, a risk the ART can't remove but everyone agrees to live with is:
questions.why: Accepted means the risk stays and the ART consciously carries it. Owned means a named person takes it away to deal with.

questions.q: Who assigns business value to team PI objectives?
questions.why: Business Owners score each objective, usually 1-10, while walking the room with each team.

questions.q: Your largest client asks for a feature that doesn't fit this quarter's roadmap theme. Best first move?
options: Build it, they're the biggest client
Understand the problem behind the request
Add it to the bottom of the backlog
questions.why: Requests arrive as solutions. Find the underlying problem first; it may fit the roadmap in a different form, or it may not matter.

questions.q: Feature A: cost of delay 20, job size 5. Feature B: cost of delay 30, job size 15. Using WSJF, which goes first?
questions.why: WSJF = cost of delay ÷ job size. A scores 4, B scores 2. Small, valuable work goes first.

questions.q: Which metric best shows that a new onboarding flow works?
options: % of new users who finish onboarding in a day
questions.why: Measure the outcome for users, not the output of the team.

questions.q: What is an MVP for?
options: Testing a hypothesis with real users
questions.why: It's the smallest thing that tells you whether you're right, not a smaller version of the full plan.

questions.q: In SAFe, who owns the ART backlog of features?
questions.why: Product Management owns ART features; Product Owners own team backlogs and stories.

questions.q: Before go-live, the best evidence that an AI feature works is:
options: Results on a labelled test set
questions.why: Agree a test set that looks like real cases and measure against it. Demos show the happy path.

questions.q: A model flags 100 cases and 60 turn out to be real. What is its precision?
questions.why: Precision = true positives ÷ all flagged = 60 ÷ 100.

questions.q: Cutting false positives hard usually risks:
questions.why: Precision and recall trade off. Tune the threshold with the business, not alone.

questions.q: Offline accuracy is 92%, but users complain. What do you check first?
options: Does test data match real use?
questions.why: A test set that doesn't look like production gives a number nobody should trust.

questions.q: Who should sign off the acceptable error rate for an AI feature?
options: Business owner with risk and compliance
questions.why: Error rates are a business and risk decision. The delivery team makes the trade-off visible.

questions.q: A team's velocity jumps 40% in one sprint. Same people, same kind of work. What do you ask first?
options: How are points being estimated now?
Can we raise next PI's targets?
Should this go in the exec report?
questions.why: A sudden jump with nothing else changing usually means estimates inflated, not output. Check before celebrating.

questions.q: The daily stand-up runs 35 minutes and sounds like a status report to the manager. Best coaching move?
options: Refocus it on the sprint goal and take details offline
Replace it with an email update
questions.why: The fix is purpose, not policy: the team talks to each other about the goal, and problem-solving happens after.

questions.q: Retro actions repeat sprint after sprint. Most likely cause?
options: Actions have no owner and never enter the next sprint backlog
questions.why: An improvement with no owner and no capacity is a wish. Put one or two actions in the next sprint with a name on each.

questions.q: Planned business value across the ART is 40; achieved is 34. What is the ART's predictability?
questions.why: 34 ÷ 40. SAFe treats roughly 80-100% as a reliable train.

questions.q: A team keeps carrying stories over sprint after sprint. Where do you look first?
options: Work in progress and story size
questions.why: Too many large stories started at once is the usual cause. Smaller slices and a WIP limit fix more than headcount.

questions.q: Two programs need the same scarce specialist in Q1. What should decide?
questions.why: Splitting a bottleneck usually slows both programs. Rank by value at portfolio level and commit.

questions.q: Earned value is 30 and actual cost is 50. What is the cost performance index (CPI)?
questions.why: CPI = EV ÷ AC. Below 1 means over budget: every 1 spent earns 0.60 of planned work.

questions.q: Earned value is 30 and planned value is 40. What is the schedule performance index (SPI)?
questions.why: SPI = EV ÷ PV. Below 1 means behind schedule.

questions.q: In Lean Portfolio Management, a large epic is ready to move forward. What does it need?
options: A lean business case reviewed through the portfolio Kanban
questions.why: Big epics go through the portfolio Kanban with a lean business case, so spend decisions are visible and deliberate.

questions.q: A senior stakeholder wants a 40-slide status deck every week. Best response?
options: Agree the few decisions and metrics they need; send one page
questions.why: Reporting should serve decisions. A one-page view of risks, asks and trends gets read; 40 slides get skimmed.

questions.q: 'Human in the loop' means:
questions.why: A person checks, corrects or approves what the AI produces before it counts.

questions.q: For a high-impact decision such as declining a customer, the safest pattern is:
questions.why: Keep the decision with an accountable person when the impact on a customer is high.

questions.q: Reviewers approve 99% of AI flags without changes. What should worry you?
questions.why: Automation bias: people stop checking. Sample reviews and track overrides.

questions.q: How do you size the human review team for an AI feature?
options: Flags per day x minutes each
questions.why: Expected review volume times handling time gives the capacity you need to plan.

questions.q: An AI agent can email customers. Minimum control before go-live?
questions.why: Anything that acts on customers needs a human gate and a way to stop it fast.

questions.q: In the I&A problem-solving workshop, what comes before brainstorming solutions?
questions.why: Fishbone or 5 Whys first; otherwise you fix symptoms.

questions.q: At the PI system demo, a feature works on one team's laptop but isn't integrated in staging. How is it counted?
questions.why: Only integrated, working increments count toward the PI.

questions.q: Three teams raise the same impediment at I&A. Best RTE move?
options: Wait one more PI to confirm
Treat it as an ART-level problem and own the fix
Let each team fix it alone
questions.why: A repeated impediment across teams is systemic. That's the RTE's to drive.

questions.q: The quantitative part of I&A mostly reviews:
questions.why: I&A looks at the system's results, never at individuals.

questions.q: Where should I&A improvement items go?
options: Into the next PI Planning backlog
questions.why: If it isn't planned with capacity, it won't happen.

questions.q: RICE: reach 2,000, impact 2, confidence 50%, effort 4. Score?
In the Kano model, a feature customers only notice when it's missing is a:
questions.why: Basics don't win customers, but missing them loses customers.

questions.q: Cheapest way to test demand before building:
questions.why: Measure behaviour, not opinions, before spending engineering time.

questions.q: Best customer-interview question:
options: Tell me about the last time you did this
questions.why: Past behaviour predicts; hypothetical answers flatter.

questions.q: An opportunity solution tree starts from:
questions.why: Outcome first, then opportunities, then solutions, then experiments.

questions.q: The EU AI Act mainly groups AI systems by:
questions.why: Rules scale with risk: banned uses, high-risk, limited-risk and minimal-risk.

questions.q: Under the EU AI Act, which group faces the strictest rules short of a ban?
questions.why: High-risk systems need risk management, data quality, logging, human oversight and documentation.

questions.q: Scoring individuals' creditworthiness with AI is, under the EU AI Act, generally:
questions.why: Credit scoring of people is listed as high-risk, which matters for banks and insurers.

questions.q: A model card documents:
questions.why: It tells users what a model is for, how it was tested and where it shouldn't be used.

questions.q: Why keep an audit trail of AI-assisted decisions?
options: To explain and review them later
questions.why: Regulators, customers and your own team will ask why a decision was made.

questions.q: A VP asks for each team's velocity to compare teams. Best response?
options: Explain velocity isn't comparable; offer outcome metrics
questions.why: Each team's points are a private scale. Comparing them invites inflation.

questions.q: A manager keeps assigning tasks to individuals in a self-organising team. First coaching step?
options: Ask what outcome they're worried about
questions.why: Control usually comes from fear of a specific risk. Address the worry, not the behaviour.

questions.q: Leadership wants 'agile' but keeps annual fixed-scope contracts. Main risk?
options: Fixed scope blocks learning from feedback
questions.why: If scope can't change, feedback has nowhere to go.

questions.q: Best sign a leader has adopted Lean-Agile thinking:
options: They ask for daily status reports
They attend system demos and act on what they see
questions.why: Going to see the real work, then removing obstacles, is the behaviour that matters.

questions.q: Servant leadership, in one phrase:
questions.why: The leader's job is to make the team's work easier, not to do it or gate it.

questions.q: RAID stands for:
questions.why: One log for everything that can derail the program.

questions.q: A risk has a 40% chance and a ₹50 lakh impact. Expected monetary value?
questions.why: 0.4 × 50. Use EMV to compare risks and size contingency.

questions.q: Difference between a risk and an issue:
options: A risk may happen; an issue already has
questions.why: Issues need action now; risks need a plan.

questions.q: Best response to a likely, high-impact risk you can't avoid:
options: Mitigate it and name an owner
questions.why: Reduce the probability or the impact, and make one person answerable.

questions.q: A (5 days) comes before B (3 days) and C (6 days); D (2 days) needs both B and C. Shortest project length?
questions.why: Critical path A → C → D = 5 + 6 + 2.

questions.q: In AI-Native SAFe, what replaces the two-day PI Planning?
questions.why: PI Outcome Planning is a one-day event focused on PI and team outcomes, ending with a confidence vote.

questions.q: ART Sense and Respond runs:
options: Once per PI, half a day
questions.why: It replaces the half-day Inspect and Adapt with a short, regular evidence review.

questions.q: Who facilitates ART Sense and Respond?
questions.why: The RTE runs it: first sensing (metrics, feedback, demos), then responding (pivots, capacity).

questions.q: ART Sense and Respond also absorbs the activities of which Core SAFe event?
questions.why: Demos of the integrated system now feed the sensing half of the event.

questions.q: Which new role does AI-Native SAFe add to the ART?
questions.why: The AI Value Architect connects business goals to AI work while weighing cost, ethics, legal and risk.

questions.q: What is the ART sync for?
options: Tracking progress and dependencies across teams
questions.why: Coach sync and PO sync keep the train's plan and dependencies honest between PI Plannings.

questions.q: A cross-team dependency slips two sprints and threatens a PI objective. First move?
options: Tell Business Owners now, with options
questions.why: Early bad news with options keeps trust; late surprises destroy it.

questions.q: Best long-term way to reduce dependencies:
questions.why: Fewer hand-offs beat better hand-off management.

questions.q: A shared DBA team is a bottleneck for five teams. Smallest effective fix?
options: Plan their capacity in PI Planning
questions.why: Make the bottleneck visible and planned before buying more of it.

questions.q: On the ART planning board, strings between cards show:
questions.why: Each string links a feature to work another team must deliver first.

questions.q: Lean budgets fund:
questions.why: Stable funding for long-lived teams removes constant re-approval.

questions.q: Lean budget guardrails are:
options: Rules keeping spend aligned with strategy
questions.why: They give freedom inside clear boundaries.

questions.q: ART capacity is 100 points and 20% is reserved for tech debt. Points left for new features?
questions.why: Capacity allocation makes the trade-off explicit before planning.

questions.q: Moving from project to value-stream funding mainly reduces:
questions.why: Teams stop waiting for each project's business case to clear.

questions.q: An epic's MVP disproves its hypothesis. Lean response?
options: Pivot or stop, and move the money
questions.why: Stopping early is the point of an MVP, not a failure.

days.topic: Running AI work on a train

questions.q: Model improvement work is hard to estimate. Best way to plan it?
questions.why: Time-box the experiment with clear exit criteria; decide to continue or stop on evidence.

questions.q: An AI feature depends on a data team in another ART. When should this surface?
options: At PI Planning, on the board
questions.why: AI work fails on data dependencies more than on models. Make them visible early.

questions.q: What should 'done' mean for an AI story?
questions.why: Done means it hits the quality bar on agreed test data and someone watches it in production.

questions.q: 'Data drift' means:
options: Real inputs move away from training data
questions.why: When the world changes, model quality drops quietly. Monitor inputs, not just uptime.

questions.q: Before teams can build a new AI feature, which enabler usually comes first?
questions.why: Without usable data there is nothing to retrieve, train on or test against.

questions.q: Flow time measures:
options: Start to done for one item
questions.why: It's the customer's wait, not the team's effort.

questions.q: WIP is 20 items and throughput is 5 items a week. Average flow time (Little's Law)?
questions.why: Flow time = WIP ÷ throughput = 20 ÷ 5.

questions.q: An item had 2 days of active work and 8 days waiting. Flow efficiency?
questions.why: Active ÷ total = 2 ÷ 10. Most waste is waiting, not working.

questions.q: Fastest lever to cut flow time:
questions.why: Little's Law again: less WIP, shorter wait, same people.

questions.q: A dashboard shows 98% of stories delivered 'on time' every sprint. What should make you curious?
options: Scope may be trimmed quietly to hit dates
questions.why: Near-perfect numbers often mean the target is being managed, not the work.

questions.q: Best North Star metric for an insurance self-service portal:
questions.why: It captures customer value and business value at once.

questions.q: 1,000 users joined in January; 600 are still active in March. Three-month retention?
questions.why: Active ÷ starting cohort.

questions.q: Survey: 50% promoters, 30% passives, 20% detractors. NPS?
questions.why: Promoters − detractors. Passives don't count.

questions.q: A vanity metric is one that:
options: Looks good but doesn't guide decisions
questions.why: If it can't change what you do next, it's decoration.

questions.q: Conversion fell after a redesign, but only on mobile. Next step?
options: Segment and check the mobile flow
questions.why: Narrow the problem before reacting to it.

questions.q: A GenAI feature costs $0.02 per request and gets 50,000 requests a day. Daily cost?
questions.why: 0.02 x 50,000 = 1,000. Usage-based costs grow with adoption, so forecast them.

questions.q: The best way to show an AI feature's value to leadership:
questions.why: Leaders fund outcomes: time saved, errors avoided, revenue protected.

questions.q: A simple, narrow task needs automation. Sensible first option?
questions.why: Use the cheapest approach that meets the quality bar; scale up only if it doesn't.

questions.q: Which usually cuts GenAI cost most for repeated questions?
questions.why: If many people ask the same thing, don't pay to generate the same answer each time.

questions.q: Why pilot an AI tool before scaling it?
options: Prove value on a small scope
questions.why: A pilot gives real numbers and surfaces risks while the cost of being wrong is small.

questions.q: 'Release on demand' means:
options: Deploy anytime, release when business wants
questions.why: Separating deploy from release lets the business choose timing.

questions.q: Feature toggles let you:
options: Deploy code without exposing it to users
questions.why: Code goes live dark, then is switched on deliberately.

questions.q: 4 of 50 deployments caused incidents. Change failure rate?
questions.why: 4 ÷ 50. One of the four DORA metrics.

questions.q: Moving from monthly to weekly releases usually needs first:
questions.why: Frequency follows automation; approvals can't scale to weekly.

questions.q: Who decides when a feature goes live to customers?
questions.why: Release is a business decision; the RTE makes sure it's possible.

questions.q: In RACI, how many people are Accountable for one task?
questions.why: Shared accountability means no accountability.

questions.q: A stakeholder with high power but low interest should be:
questions.why: Low effort, but never surprise them.

questions.q: You learn of a two-week slip. When do you tell the sponsor?
questions.why: Early bad news with options is a planning input; late bad news is a crisis.

questions.q: Status was green for six months, then suddenly red. What failed?
questions.why: Watermelon status: green outside, red inside.

questions.q: How many communication channels in a team of 10?
questions.why: n(n − 1) ÷ 2 = 10 × 9 ÷ 2. Why big teams struggle.

questions.q: Prompt injection is:
questions.why: Text inside a document, email or web page tells the model to ignore its rules or leak data.

questions.q: An AI agent reads customer emails and can take actions. Biggest new risk?
questions.why: Anything the agent reads can carry instructions. Treat inputs as data, never as commands.

questions.q: Safest default for an AI agent's access to tools and data:
questions.why: Give the agent only what the task needs, and log what it does.

questions.q: Before sending customer data to an external AI service, check:
questions.why: Contracts, data residency and privacy law decide what may leave your systems.

questions.q: 'Red teaming' an AI feature means:
options: Trying to make it fail on purpose
questions.why: Testers attack the system with misuse and tricky inputs before real users do.

questions.q: In retros, people only say positive things. Likely signal?
questions.why: Silence about problems usually means it doesn't feel safe to raise them.

questions.q: Two senior engineers clash over architecture in every refinement. Best move?
options: Facilitate a session with agreed decision criteria
questions.why: Agree how to decide before arguing what to decide.

questions.q: A team member admits a mistake that caused an outage. Best first response?
options: Thank them and run a blameless review
Name them in the incident report
questions.why: Punish honesty once and you'll never hear about problems early again.

questions.q: Tuckman's 'storming' stage is:
options: A sign to break up the team
questions.why: Every team passes through it; the coach helps it pass quickly.

questions.q: Remote team, cameras off, little discussion. First step?
options: Ask the team what would help
questions.why: Start with their view of the problem before imposing a fix.

questions.q: Which is a good key result?
questions.why: Measurable outcome, not an activity or a wish.

questions.q: Key result: cut onboarding from 10 days to 3. You reached 5. Progress?
Portfolio strategic themes are:
options: Business objectives that steer the portfolio
questions.why: They connect strategy to what gets funded.

questions.q: Should OKRs be tied directly to pay?
questions.why: When pay depends on hitting them, people set safe targets.

questions.q: Typical number of objectives per team per quarter:
questions.why: Few enough to say no to everything else.

questions.q: Teams ignore a new AI assistant. First move?
questions.why: Low adoption usually means it doesn't fit the daily work yet. Find out why before pushing.

questions.q: Best adoption metric for an internal AI tool:
questions.why: Count repeat use on real work, not purchases or attendance.

questions.q: Leaders want AI 'everywhere' this quarter. Best advice from the RTE?
questions.why: Focus proves value and builds the patterns other teams can reuse.

questions.q: Who should own the business outcome of an AI use case?
questions.why: Someone accountable on the business side decides whether it is working and worth the cost.

questions.q: Staff fear AI will replace them. Most effective response?
questions.why: Honest communication plus skills support builds trust; empty promises break it.

questions.q: A team wants an AI assistant to draft user stories. Key control?
questions.why: AI can draft; people stay accountable for what's committed.

questions.q: An AI screening step cut false positives from 30% to 15%. Relative reduction?
questions.why: (30 − 15) ÷ 30. Absolute drop is 15 points; relative drop is half.

questions.q: Before scaling an AI feature across the ART, the RTE should ensure:
options: Clear success metrics and a governance owner
questions.why: Without a metric and an owner, nobody can say if it works or stop it if it doesn't.

questions.q: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mainly helps by:
options: Grounding answers in your own documents
questions.why: It fetches relevant content first, so answers cite your sources.

questions.q: Biggest testing challenge with AI features:
options: Outputs vary for the same input
questions.why: Non-deterministic output needs evaluation sets, not just pass/fail tests.

questions.q: Function points measure:
questions.why: Size from the user's view, independent of language.

questions.q: 400 function points at 8 hours each. Effort?
questions.why: 400 × 8. Calibrate the rate with your own past data.

questions.q: A fixed-price vendor contract fits best when:
questions.why: Fixed price punishes change; use it where change is unlikely.

questions.q: The cone of uncertainty says early estimates are:
questions.why: Ranges should narrow as you learn; give ranges early.

questions.q: What most improves estimate accuracy quickly?
questions.why: Your own history beats expert guesses.
